words: force; push; pull; balanced; unbalanced; direction; gravity; motion; fair test; variable
notes: Plan and run, as a class at first and then in small groups, a fair test of what a push or pull does to an object's motion: change one thing at a time (how many pushes, how strong compared with another, which direction) and keep the rest the same. Balanced forces (equal pushes from both sides on a box) give no change in motion; an unbalanced force starts, stops, speeds up or turns an object. Introduces the force arrow drawing (an arrow shows the direction of a push or pull, a longer arrow a stronger one) as a model students revise. Gravity is named as a pull toward the ground. Boundary: one variable at a time; force size is compared, never measured in units; gravity only as a pull down. First fair test of the band (Appendix F, 3-5 investigations). Skips grade 4 to s5-gravity-down because grade 4 has no forces standard; grade 4's s4-collisions carries the force arrow so the model has no gap.

words: motion; pattern; predict; observe; measure; record; swing; back and forth
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.4 (measuring lengths to the half and quarter inch for how far an object moves)
notes: Observe and measure motion that repeats (a swing, a ball rolling back and forth in a bowl, a see-saw, a pendulum of string and washers) and record it in a table so the pattern shows; use the pattern to predict where the object will be next and test the prediction. The reasoning that grows: a pattern in the data lets you predict, and a prediction that fails tells you something changed. Boundary: no technical words such as period or frequency. Hands on to s4-speed-energy the habit of describing motion by how fast and how far.

words: magnet; attract; repel; pole; static electricity; charge; distance; non-contact force
cross_subject: ela:SL.3.1 (asking and answering questions in a collaborative discussion)
notes: Ask testable questions about pushes and pulls between objects that do not touch, then investigate them: magnet to magnet, magnet to steel paper clips, one magnet against two, a charged balloon and hair or bits of paper. Cause and effect to find: closer objects push or pull more strongly, and turning a magnet around changes attract to repel. Force arrows are drawn between objects that are not touching. Boundary: only objects students can handle; electric effects only as static electricity (no circuits here). Teacher note: small and strong magnets are a swallowing hazard for young children and harm devices and cards; count magnets out and back. Skips grade 4 to s5-gravity-down (gravity also pulls without touching), since grade 4 teaches no forces standard.

words: design problem; need; want; criteria; constraint; materials; cost; time; solution
cross_subject: math:3.MD.A.2 (measuring masses in grams when a criterion is how much the latch must hold)
notes: Define a simple design problem that magnets can solve (a latch that keeps a cupboard door shut, a way to keep two moving toy cars from touching), written as the need, the criteria for success and the constraints on materials, time and cost. The band's engineering standard 3-5-ETS1-1 is done in full here: students state the problem precisely enough that two solutions could be judged against it. They may sketch and try one solution, but comparing many solutions is grade 4 (s4-information-codes, 3-5-ETS1-2) and fair tests of a prototype are grade 5 (s5-design-test, 3-5-ETS1-3). Grade 3's other design work, judging the merit of solutions in s3-environment-change-solution and s3-weather-hazard, uses the criteria language set here. Teacher note: the magnet swallowing and device warnings of s3-magnet-static apply.

words: life cycle; birth; growth; reproduction; death; seed; egg; larva; adult; flowering plant
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.7 (using diagrams and illustrations to understand a text)
notes: Develop models (drawn cycles, sequenced cards, a class chart) of life cycles of several organisms, watched where possible (bean or radish plants, mealworms or butterflies), and compare them: every cycle differs in its stages and timing, yet all share birth, growth, reproduction and death. The changes form a pattern. Students revise the model when observation shows a stage they missed. Boundary: plant life cycles are flowering plants only; human reproduction is not included. Teacher note: care for living things humanely and return or release them as local rules allow; check allergies before handling plants, soil or insects.

words: group; herd; flock; pack; colony; survive; protect; claim; evidence; reason
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (writing an opinion with reasons that support it)
notes: Construct an argument, with a claim, evidence and reasoning, that some animals form groups that help their members survive: wolves hunt in packs, fish school, bees divide work, musk oxen circle against predators. Evidence comes from video, data on hunting success or survival in groups and alone, and readings. The reasoning that grows: the claim is about cause (being in a group makes survival more likely), and some animals live alone and survive in other ways, which a good argument admits. Social interactions only at the level of what the group does, no animal behavior mechanisms.

words: trait; inherit; parent; offspring; sibling; variation; similar; different
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (scaled bar graphs to compare how many offspring show each trait)
notes: Analyze and interpret data (photos, tallies, bar graphs) to show that young plants and animals have traits like their parents and that individuals of the same kind still vary: puppies in a litter, kittens, seedlings from one packet, ear length in rabbits. Patterns to find are the likenesses between parents and offspring and the differences among siblings. Boundary: no genes or other mechanism of inheritance, no predicting traits, and non-human examples only (so no student is asked about family resemblance). Sets up s3-environment-traits, which separates inherited traits from traits the environment shapes.

words: environment; influence; inherited; grown; stunted; evidence; explanation
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.4 (measuring plant heights in inches and halves of inches)
notes: Use evidence to support the explanation that the environment can change a trait: the same kind of plant grown with too little water or light is shorter and paler; a dog fed too much and walked too little gets heavy; flamingos fed less shrimp turn paler. A class plant investigation (same seeds, one condition changed) gives first-hand evidence. Comes after s3-inherited-traits in the year so students can sort traits into inherited, shaped by the environment, or both. Teacher note: do not use people's weight or bodies as examples. Skips grade 4 to s5-plant-matter: grade 4 has no plant growth standard, and grade 5 reuses this plant-growth investigation to ask where the plant's matter comes from.

words: fossil; extinct; environment; long ago; ancient; layer; marine; relative age
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.7 (reading information from pictures, maps and charts of fossil finds)
notes: Analyze and interpret data from fossils (kind, size and where they are found) as evidence of the organisms that lived long ago and the environments they lived in: sea shells on dry land show sea once covered it, tropical plant fossils in the Arctic show a once-warm climate, and fossils of extinct organisms show living things have changed. Older fossils lie deeper in undisturbed layers, so ages are relative. Boundary: no naming of specific fossils or modern species to memorize; major fossil types and relative age only. BASELINE rule 5: Earth's long history is stated as the evidence shows. Hands on to s4-rock-layers, which uses fossils in rock layers to explain how a landscape changed.

words: variation; advantage; survive; camouflage; predator; prey; mate; offspring; characteristic
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.3 (describing cause and effect relationships in a science text)
notes: Use evidence to build an explanation for how differences among individuals of one kind give some of them an advantage in surviving, finding mates and having young: plants with larger thorns are eaten less, better-camouflaged moths are found by birds less often (a camouflage hunt with colored paper on a patterned background gives class data). The reasoning that grows: a small difference, through cause and effect, changes who survives and leaves offspring. Structure and function returns from K-2 (thorns, coloring). No natural selection by name and no genetics; that is grade 8 (MS-LS4-4).

words: habitat; survive; need; ecosystem; system; depend; adapted; food; shelter
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (an opinion piece with reasons, here a claim about a habitat)
notes: Construct an argument with evidence that in a given habitat some organisms survive well, some less well and some not at all, using the organisms' needs and characteristics and the habitat's conditions (a cactus in a desert and in a bog, a polar bear and a frog in the Arctic). The organisms and their habitat form a system whose parts depend on each other, so the system model from K-2 grows here. Skips grade 4 to s5-matter-movement: grade 4 has no ecosystem standard, and grade 5's model of matter moving in an ecosystem builds on this habitat-as-system idea.

words: environmental change; habitat; solution; merit; criteria; migrate; problem
cross_subject: ela:RI.3.8 (connecting sentences and paragraphs in a text to see cause and effect)
notes: Make a claim about the merit of a solution to a problem caused when an environment changes and the plants and animals there change too: wildlife crossings over a new highway, a fish ladder at a dam, replanting after a fire. Students judge each solution against criteria stated the way s3-design-problem taught. Boundary: a single environmental change at a time; the greenhouse effect and climate change are not assessed here. BASELINE rule 5: if students raise climate change, answer it plainly as the evidence shows; it is taught in grades 6 to 8. Strand life because the core idea is LS4.D; the design reasoning is engineering practice.

words: weather; season; temperature; precipitation; wind direction; average; table; bar graph; pictograph
cross_subject: math:3.MD.B.3 (scaled picture graphs and bar graphs)
notes: Represent weather data in tables, pictographs and bar graphs to describe the weather typical of each season in a place: monthly average temperature, rainfall or snowfall, and wind direction, from the class's own weather log and from local records. The reasoning that grows: one day's weather is not a season's; typical conditions come from many days. Boundary: graphs limited to pictographs and bar graphs; climate change is not assessed. Paced after grade 3 math has taught scaled bar graphs (3.MD.B.3). Hands on to s4-weathering-erosion the habit of recording measurements in a table and graphing them.

words: climate; region; weather; equator; pole; tropical; desert; polar; temperate
cross_subject: social-studies:ss3-globe-grid (equator and poles on the globe, why places near the equator are warm); ela:RI.3.9 (comparing the key points of two texts on one topic)
notes: Obtain and combine information from texts, maps and data to describe the climates of different regions of the world, and tell climate (the pattern over many years) from weather (today). Patterns to find: warm near the equator and cold near the poles, wet and dry places. Comes after s3-weather-data in the year so typical conditions are already a known idea. No climate causes (the sun's angle, ocean currents) beyond the pattern. Skips grade 4 to s5-sphere-interactions, because grade 4 has no weather or climate standard and grade 5 explains how ocean and air shape climate.

words: hazard; flood; storm; lightning; barrier; levee; lightning rod; design solution; merit; reduce
cross_subject: ela:W.3.1 (opinion writing with reasons, here a claim about a design)
notes: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impact of a weather-related hazard (a flood barrier, a wind-resistant roof, a lightning rod), judged against criteria and constraints. Students may build and test a quick model (a roof that stays on under a fan) to give their claim evidence. Humans cannot stop severe weather but can lessen its harm. Teacher note: some students may have lived through floods, fires or storms; keep examples general and let students choose whether to share. Hands on to s4-hazard-solutions, which generates and compares several solutions for earthquakes, floods and volcanoes.

words: energy; speed; faster; slower; motion energy; evidence; explanation
cross_subject: ela:W.4.2 (an informative text that explains with facts and details)
notes: Use evidence to build an explanation relating an object's speed to its energy: a faster ball knocks a cup farther, a faster cart makes a louder bump. Energy is introduced as something a moving object has more of when it moves faster. Boundary: speed is compared (faster, slower), never calculated, and energy is not given a precise or number definition. Assumes from s3-motion-patterns the habit of describing motion by how far and how fast. Comes first in grade 4 physical science; s4-energy-transfer then follows energy as it moves.

words: energy; transfer; heat; light; sound; electric current; circuit; battery; conductor
notes: Make observations that give evidence energy moves from place to place by sound (a drum makes rice on another drum jump), light (sunlight warms a dark cloth), heat (a warm hand warms a cold spoon) and electric current (a battery, wires and a bulb or buzzer in a closed circuit). Introduces the energy transfer model: a drawing with arrows that follows energy from where it starts to where it goes. Boundary: no number measurements of energy. Teacher note: use only low-voltage batteries; never household outlets; a battery wired straight to itself (a short circuit) gets hot, so the bulb or buzzer is always in the loop; no lenses aimed at skin. Hands on to s5-food-energy-sun, where the arrows follow energy from the sun into food.

words: collide; collision; energy; transfer; speed; predict; contact force
notes: Ask questions and predict outcomes about how energy changes when objects collide: a rolling marble hits a still one, a toy car hits a block, the faster one before the collision gives more motion, sound or warmth after. Emphasis is on the change in energy that comes with the change in speed, not on the forces; the force arrows of s3-balanced-forces appear only to show the push at contact that passes energy on. Boundary: no number measurements of energy. Teacher note: rolling objects at low speed, on the floor or a table edge guard; no throwing. Comes after s4-energy-transfer so the energy arrow is already a known model.

words: device; convert; design; test; refine; prototype; criteria; constraint; stored energy
cross_subject: math:4.OA.A.3 (multistep word problems when a design has a budget of materials)
notes: Apply energy ideas to design, test and refine a device that changes energy from one form to another: a circuit that drives a small motor car, lights a bulb or sounds a buzzer; a rubber-band or spring car using stored energy; a passive solar heater (a box that turns sunlight into warmth). Constraints are the materials, cost and time. This row starts 3-5-ETS1-3: students test their device, find where it fails and improve it, but without the planned fair test with controlled variables that s5-design-test completes. Boundary: devices change motion into electric energy or use stored energy to cause motion, light or sound. Teacher note: low-voltage batteries only, no outlets; watch for hot wires in a short circuit; solar heaters can get hot, use a thermometer, not a hand.

words: wave; amplitude; wavelength; peak; crest; trough; vibration; pattern
cross_subject: math:4.G.A.1 (drawing points, lines and line segments to mark a wave and its wavelength)
notes: Develop a model of waves (a drawing, a rope or slinky wave, a wave machine of straws and tape, ripples in a tray of water) to describe them by their patterns: amplitude (how tall) and wavelength (peak to peak), and to show that waves make things move (a floating cork bobs up and down but is not carried away). Introduces the wave model, built on K-2's sound and vibration work (1-PS4-1). Boundary: no interference, no light or other electromagnetic waves as waves, no single non-repeating waves, no number models of amplitude or wavelength. Teacher note: water trays on a covered table; wipe spills at once. Hands on to grade 8 sound waves (MS-PS4-1), across the band.

words: light; reflect; eye; source; path; mirror; see; object
cross_subject: ela:SL.4.5 (adding a drawing or visual display to a spoken explanation)
notes: Develop a model that shows we see an object because light from a source bounces off the object and travels into the eye: drawn rays with arrows from lamp to object to eye, tested with mirrors, a flashlight in a box with a peephole and a dark room. The common idea that light goes out from the eye is tested and revised with evidence. Introduces a new model name, light-path (the arrows light follows), because none of the shared names fits: it is not a wave model at this grade. Boundary: not which colors are reflected, no cells of the eye or how the retina works. Teacher note: never look at the sun, even through a mirror; no lasers. Hands on to s5-star-brightness and to grade 6 light and matter (MS-PS4-2), across the band.

words: code; signal; pattern; information; transfer; Morse code; grid; pixel; compare; solution
cross_subject: math:4.OA.C.5 (making and following a pattern by a rule)
notes: Generate and compare several solutions that use patterns to send information: drum beats in a code across the field, a grid of 1s and 0s that sends a black and white picture, flashlight Morse code. Each team builds two or more codes and judges them against shared criteria (speed, errors, distance) and constraints. 3-5-ETS1-2 is done in full here: students produce more than one solution and compare how well each is likely to meet the criteria, building on the problem definition of s3-design-problem. s4-hazard-solutions uses the same comparison. Comes after s4-wave-model so sound and light signals are known as waves that carry a pattern.

words: structure; function; internal; external; organ; heart; lung; stomach; brain; skin; root; stem; petal; thorn
cross_subject: ela:W.4.1 (an opinion piece supported by reasons and information)
notes: Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that work to support survival, growth, behavior and reproduction: roots take in water, thorns protect, colored petals draw pollinators, the heart pumps blood, lungs take in air, skin protects. Each structure is part of a larger system in the body or plant. Assumes s3-life-cycles (reproduction as a stage the structures serve) and s3-variation-advantage (a difference in a structure can help survival). Boundary: structures that can be seen without a microscope; no cells. Hands on to s5-plant-matter the idea that leaves and roots take in materials, and to grade 6 cells and body systems (MS-LS1-3), across the band.

words: sense; senses; brain; nerve; signal; information; respond; react; memory
cross_subject: ela:SL.4.5 (a visual display that makes an explanation clear)
notes: Use a model to describe how animals take in different kinds of information through their senses, process it in the brain and respond in different ways: a flow model from sense organ to brain to action, tested with reaction-time games (catching a dropped ruler) and examples from other animals (an owl hearing prey, a snake sensing heat). Emphasis on how information moves through a system. Boundary: not how the brain stores and recalls memories, nor how sense receptors work. Comes after s4-structures-function so the sense organs are known structures. Hands on to grade 6 (MS-LS1-8), across the band.

words: rock layer; fossil; landscape; canyon; erosion; older; younger; change over time; evidence
cross_subject: ela:W.4.7 (a short research project that builds knowledge of a topic)
notes: Identify evidence from patterns in rock layers and the fossils in them to explain how a landscape changed over time: shell fossils in a layer above plant fossils show land became sea; a canyon with layered walls and a river at the bottom shows the river cut through the rock. Lower layers in undisturbed rock are older (relative time). Assumes s3-fossils (fossils show past organisms and environments). Boundary: not how rocks form, no memorizing named formations, relative time only. BASELINE rule 5: the great age of the Earth is stated as the evidence shows. Hands on to grade 6 rock cycling (MS-ESS1-4, MS-ESS2-2), across the band.

words: weathering; erosion; deposition; slope; sediment; rate; freeze; thaw; variable; measure
cross_subject: math:4.MD.A.1 (knowing relative sizes of units when measuring how far sediment moves)
notes: Make observations and measurements that give evidence of weathering, or of the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind or plants: a stream table or sloped tray of sand with the slope, water amount or plant cover changed one at a time; freezing and thawing a wet clay or plaster block; shaking rocks in a jar. Data go in tables and bar graphs, built on s3-weather-data. Boundary: one kind of weathering or erosion at a time. Teacher note: water and sand on covered tables; wash hands after handling soil. Hands on to s5-sphere-interactions (water and wind shaping land is two Earth systems interacting).

words: map; topographic; mountain; volcano; earthquake; ocean floor; continent; boundary; trench; pattern
cross_subject: ela:RI.4.7 (interpreting information shown in maps, charts and diagrams); social-studies:ss4-state-maps (reading physical maps of a state)
notes: Analyze and interpret maps to describe patterns in Earth's features: topographic maps of land and the ocean floor, and maps that place mountains, continental edges, volcanoes and earthquakes. The pattern to find: mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes line up in belts, often along the edges of continents, and the ocean floor has mountain ranges and trenches. No plate tectonics by name; the pattern is left as a question that grade 6 answers (MS-ESS2-3, the plate model), across the band. Hands on to s5-water-distribution the map reading of oceans, ice and land.

words: natural resource; fuel; fossil fuel; renewable; nonrenewable; wind; solar; dam; pollution; environment
cross_subject: ela:W.4.8 (gathering information from print and digital sources and taking notes); social-studies:ss4-regions-resources (natural resources of US regions)
notes: Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels come from natural resources and that using them affects the environment. Renewable: wind, water behind dams, sunlight. Nonrenewable: fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and the fuel used in nuclear power plants. Effects: habitat lost to dams and surface mines, air pollution from burning fossil fuels. Uses the energy transfer arrows from s4-energy-transfer. Assumes s3-environment-change-solution (a change to the environment changes what lives there). Facts and backed sources decide claims (values rule b); no resource is cheered or blamed beyond what the evidence shows. Hands on to s5-protect-resources.

words: natural hazard; earthquake; flood; tsunami; volcano; eruption; warning; monitor; reduce; impact
cross_subject: ela:RI.4.9 (combining information from two texts on the same topic); social-studies:ss4-disasters-response (how communities respond to disasters)
notes: Generate and compare several solutions that reduce the effects of natural Earth processes on people: an earthquake-resistant building (tested on a shake table of a tray and rubber balls), better monitoring of a volcano, tsunami warnings, flood walls. Builds on s3-weather-hazard (judging one solution) by producing and comparing several, as s4-information-codes taught; uses s4-earth-feature-maps to see where hazards cluster. Boundary: earthquakes, floods, tsunamis and volcanic eruptions only. Teacher note: some students may have lived through a disaster; keep examples general and let students choose whether to share. Hands on to s5-design-test.

words: matter; particle; too small to see; gas; air; dissolve; evaporate; compress; model
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.7 (drawing on several print and digital sources to answer a question)
notes: Develop a model that matter is made of particles too small to be seen, from evidence the class gathers: pumping air into a ball makes it firmer and heavier; air in a closed syringe can be squeezed; sugar dissolved in water vanishes from sight but the water tastes sweet; salt water left to dry leaves salt behind. Introduces the particle model (dots drawn for parts too small to see, closer or farther apart) and the idea of very small scale. Students revise their first drawings as each piece of evidence arrives. Boundary: no atoms or molecules by name, no particle-level account of evaporation and condensation. Teacher note: never taste in the lab; the teacher does any tasting demonstration with food-safe materials, or it is described. Hands on to grade 6 thermal energy (MS-PS1-4), across the band.

words: weight; conserve; total; scale; gram; melt; freeze; dissolve; mix; before; after
cross_subject: math:5.MD.A.1 (converting grams and kilograms within one system)
notes: Measure and graph weights to give evidence that when substances are heated, cooled or mixed, the total weight stays the same, whatever the change: ice melting in a sealed bag, salt dissolving in water, baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bottle with a balloon on top. Data go in a before and after table and bar graph; a change in weight is traced to something escaping (a gas), which the particle model explains. Boundary: mass and weight are not told apart. Teacher note: eye protection for any fizzing mix; seal only with a balloon or loose cap, never a tight lid, so pressure cannot build. Comes after s5-particles.

words: property; material; hardness; color; reflect; conduct; magnetic; dissolve; solubility; identify
cross_subject: ela:W.5.8 (recording information and summarizing it in notes)
notes: Make observations and measurements to identify materials by their properties: white powders (baking soda, cornstarch, sugar, salt), metals, minerals and liquids, tested for color, hardness, shine, whether they conduct electricity or heat, whether a magnet pulls them and whether they dissolve. Students build a property table and use its pattern to name an unknown sample. Boundary: density is not used as a property; mass and weight are not told apart. Teacher note: eye protection; no tasting; powders kept from the eyes and mouth; wash hands after. Builds on K-2's sorting by property (2-PS1-1), across the band.

words: mix; mixture; new substance; change; gas; bubbles; property; evidence
cross_subject: ela:W.5.7 (a short research project using several sources)
notes: Conduct an investigation to decide whether mixing two or more substances makes a new substance: new properties (bubbles of a new gas, a color change, a solid forming, warmth) are evidence of a new substance, while a mixture that can be separated again (sand and salt, iron filings and sand) is not. Students plan which mixes to test and what counts as evidence. Comes after s5-identify-materials so properties are known tools. Teacher note: eye protection for all mixing; only kitchen-safe substances (baking soda, vinegar, milk, lemon juice, cornstarch, steel wool and water), never household cleaners; no tasting. Hands on to grade 7 chemical reactions (MS-PS1-2), across the band.

words: gravity; force; down; center; Earth; sphere; pull; argument
cross_subject: ela:W.5.1 (opinion writing supported by logically ordered reasons)
notes: Support an argument that Earth's gravity pulls objects down, where down means toward the center of the round Earth: plumb lines and dropped objects everywhere fall toward the ground, and on a globe that is toward the middle, so 'down' in Australia points a different way in space than 'down' here. Force arrows from s3-balanced-forces now point toward Earth's center. Assumes s3-balanced-forces (gravity as a pull down, force arrows) and s3-magnet-static (a pull without touching); both skip grade 4 because grade 4 teaches no forces standard. Boundary: no math for gravity. Hands on to grade 8 forces at a distance (MS-PS2-4), across the band.

words: energy; food; sun; sunlight; plant; animal; body warmth; growth; flow chart
cross_subject: ela:SL.5.5 (adding visual displays to a presentation)
notes: Use models (diagrams, flow charts) to describe that the energy in animals' food, used for growth, repair, motion and keeping warm, was once energy from the sun: sun to grass to cow to person, each arrow an energy transfer. Uses the energy transfer arrows of s4-energy-transfer and the food web drawn in s5-matter-movement, and keeps energy (which flows through) apart from matter (which cycles). No photosynthesis chemistry. Hands on to grade 7 matter and energy in organisms (MS-LS1-6, MS-LS2-3), across the band.

words: plant; matter; growth; air; water; soil; carbon dioxide; argument; evidence
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.9 (combining information from several texts on one topic); math:5.MD.A.1 (comparing weights in grams and kilograms)
notes: Support an argument that plants get the materials they need to grow chiefly from air and water, not from soil: the historical tree-in-a-pot data (soil weight barely changes while the tree gains many kilograms), plants grown in water alone, and the class's own weighed soil before and after. The particle model of s5-particles makes air a kind of matter that can become plant. Assumes s3-environment-traits (plants grown short of water are stunted) and s4-structures-function (roots and leaves take in materials). Emphasis is on where plant matter comes from; light is the energy, not the material. Teacher note: check allergies to plants, soil and mold. Comes after s5-particles.

words: ecosystem; producer; consumer; decomposer; food web; matter; cycle; soil; nutrient; environment
cross_subject: ela:RI.5.7 (drawing on several sources to answer a question)
notes: Develop a model of matter moving among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment: plants make food from air and water; animals eat plants or other animals; decomposers break dead matter into soil, air and water that plants use again. Introduces the food web (who eats whom, with decomposers) and the matter cycle (matter goes round and is used again); a sealed jar ecosystem or a compost bottle gives first-hand evidence over weeks. Assumes s3-habitat-survival (a habitat as a system whose parts depend on each other), a skip because grade 4 has no ecosystem standard. Boundary: no molecules. Teacher note: keep compost bottles closed; wash hands; mold allergies. Hands on to grade 7 matter cycling and ecosystems (MS-LS2-3), across the band.

words: shadow; length; direction; day; night; rotate; orbit; season; star; constellation; pattern
cross_subject: math:5.G.A.2 (graphing points on the coordinate plane to show how a shadow changes over a day)
notes: Represent data in graphs to reveal daily and seasonal patterns: a shadow stick's shadow measured each hour (length and direction), day length through the year, and stars or constellations seen only in some months. Introduces the Earth-sun-moon model as Earth spinning (day and night, moving shadows) and moving around the sun (different night-sky stars by season), checked with a globe and lamp. Boundary: the causes of seasons are not taught (grade 8, MS-ESS1-1). Teacher note: never look at the sun, even briefly or through tinted glass. If the K to 2 part already hands on earth-sun-moon (1-ESS1-1), the stitcher makes this a carry; grades 3 and 4 have no sky standard, so the model rests there.

words: star; sun; brightness; apparent; distance; near; far; light year
cross_subject: math:5.NBT.A.2 (powers of ten for very large distances)
notes: Support an argument that the sun looks far brighter than other stars because it is much closer to Earth: two equal flashlights at different distances in a dark hall give evidence, and star distance data in powers of ten show the scale. Uses the light-path model of s4-light-eye (light from the star travels to the eye; less of it arrives from farther away). The sun is a star. Boundary: relative distance only; not star size, mass, age or stage. Comes after s5-shadows-sky. Hands on to grade 8 Earth in space (MS-ESS1-3), across the band.

words: geosphere; hydrosphere; atmosphere; biosphere; system; interact; climate; landform; ocean
cross_subject: ela:SL.5.5 (a visual display in a presentation)
notes: Develop a model, through one worked example, of how two of Earth's systems interact: the ocean shapes coastlines and local climate and supports life; rain and wind wear down land; mountains force air up so clouds form on one side. Each of rock and land, water, air and living things is a system. Assumes s4-weathering-erosion (water and wind change land) and s3-climates (climate regions, a skip since grade 4 has no climate standard). Boundary: two systems at a time. Hands on to grade 6 weather, climate and water cycling (MS-ESS2-4, MS-ESS2-6), across the band.

words: salt water; fresh water; ocean; glacier; ice cap; groundwater; lake; river; percent; reservoir
cross_subject: math:4.NF.C.6 (hundredths as decimals, for the share of Earth's water in each place)
notes: Describe and graph how much of Earth's water is salt water and how much is fresh, and where the fresh water is: about 97 of every 100 parts in the ocean, most fresh water locked in glaciers and ice caps or underground, and very little in lakes and rivers. A bar graph and a hundred-square grid make the scale visible. Assumes s4-earth-feature-maps (reading maps of oceans and ice). Boundary: oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, groundwater and polar ice only; water in the air is not included. Comes after s5-sphere-interactions. Hands on to s5-protect-resources the case that usable fresh water is scarce.

words: resource; protect; conserve; pollution; community; recycle; habitat; solution
cross_subject: ela:W.5.8 (gathering information from print and digital sources)
notes: Obtain and combine information about how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources and environment: protecting watersheds, cleaning up runoff, restoring wetlands, cutting air pollution, saving water. Students connect each action to the Earth system it protects. Assumes s4-energy-resources (using resources affects the environment). Uses the fresh water case from s5-water-distribution. Facts and backed sources decide claims (values rule b). Supplies the design problem for s5-design-test. Hands on to grade 7 human impact (MS-ESS3-3), across the band.

words: fair test; variable; control; trial; failure point; prototype; improve; criteria; constraint
cross_subject: math:5.MD.B.2 (line plots of repeated measurements in fractions of a unit)
notes: The band's full design cycle, completing 3-5-ETS1-3: define a problem from s5-protect-resources (for example a filter that cleans muddy water, or a device that catches rain runoff), generate and compare solutions, then plan and run fair tests of the prototype in which one variable changes and the rest are held the same, with several trials, and find the failure points that show what to improve. s4-energy-device started this standard by testing and refining a device; here the fair test is planned and the data are graphed before a change is made. Assumes s4-energy-device, s4-information-codes and s4-hazard-solutions. Teacher note: filtered water is never drunk; gloves for muddy or runoff water; wash hands. Hands on to grade 6 to 8 engineering (MS-ETS1-3, MS-ETS1-4), across the band.
